Lesson 9 · Evaluate the action

How much did alerts help those stores?

Lesson 8 reconstructed why these stores adopted alerts and compared broad delivery-time groups. We now use their measured starting conditions to estimate the gain for the whole voluntary cohort.

Voluntary cohort · S051–S100 · outcome weeks 17–24

Method in this decision: Adjustment and matching

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The decision brief

The director wants an expansion estimate for all 50 stores in the voluntary cohort, including those that did not adopt. The observed adopter comparison mixes the policy with differences in their starting conditions. We will use a model to predict both options for the same stores. The essential calculation is visible: make two predictions per store, subtract them, and average the differences over the population covered by the budget.

Follow the analysis

  2. Keep the target stores fixed

Begin by specifying the experiment we would like to run

Reconstruct the target trial in words

  • Eligibility: the 50 stores in the voluntary cohort.
  • Decision time: before adoption begins in week 17.
  • Options: offer alerts or continue usual operations.
  • Follow-up: weeks 17–24; outcome: average stockout rate.

Observational analysis is often necessary because management cannot randomize every policy. Specifying the ideal experiment clarifies which records, times, and variables belong in the comparison. The practical target is the effect for the stores covered by the proposed budget.

Identify why assignment may be endogenous

Three ways the observed comparison can be distorted
MechanismRetail example
Common causeDelivery problems affect adoption and future stockouts.
Reverse directionManagers adopt because stockout pressure is already rising.
Measurement errorA noisy baseline fails to represent an important starting condition.

Externally assigned variation and voluntary choices can coexist. The assignment mechanism determines which comparisons are credible. Avoid adjusting for a mechanism after treatment or selecting on a common consequence; those choices can change or distort the target established in the preceding lesson.

Separate internal from external validity

  • Internal: does the comparison identify the effect for the study population?
  • External: how does that evidence apply to the stores targeted next?

A well-designed estimate can still need adaptation for a new population. Make sample restrictions, missing-data decisions, and coding choices explicit. Selecting stores with complete starting records or trimming extreme profiles changes the population whose effect is estimated.

Keep the target stores fixed

There is one analysis row per store. The outcome is that store’s average stockout rate in weeks 17–24. The pre-policy fields are usual delivery time, urban location, and baseline stockout rate from weeks 1–8. The adoption flag records which stores began alerts in week 17.

These are the same 50 stores discussed in Lesson 8. The randomized pilot stores do not enter this fit. Keeping the study populations separate lets the director understand why their estimates may differ: the delivery-time mix and the way alerts were assigned differ between cohorts.

The target for this calculation is an equal-weight average across all 50 voluntary-cohort stores. Each store receives one vote because the proposed budget offers the same weekly service to each store.

Predict the same store under both options

Fit the stockout rate using the adoption flag and the three starting characteristics. Add interactions between adoption and delivery time, and between adoption and urban location. An interaction allows the alert difference to vary across store types.

Now copy each store’s model inputs twice. In the first copy, set the adoption flag to zero; in the second, set it to one. Keep delivery time, location, and the baseline rate identical across the copies. The subtraction is usual-operation prediction minus alert prediction, so a positive number is a reduction in stockouts.

Read the estimate for the decision population

The model-adjusted reduction is 3.01 percentage points, with a model-based 95% interval from 2.39 to 3.63. The raw usual-minus-adopter gap was 2.06. Adjustment changes the comparison by asking both policy questions of the same target stores.

If we average those paired predictions only over stores that adopted, the estimate becomes 3.38 points. The calculation has not changed its definition of a store-level reduction; it has changed whose reductions are averaged. Use the all-store result for an all-store offer and the adopter result for a question about current users.

The model uses the pre-policy selection variables identified in Lesson 8. Its interval describes uncertainty in this fitted comparison. Reviewing the operational assignment story remains part of choosing the design, while the table makes the numerical step inspectable.

Compare adjustment tools using their actual retained stores

Read progressively richer regressions on the same sample

Same voluntary cohort and follow-up outcome
SpecificationReduction95% model interval
Unadjusted2.061.00 to 3.13
Starting conditions2.902.21 to 3.60
Heterogeneous, standardized3.012.39 to 3.63

The first model is the raw difference. The second adjusts for delivery time, location, and baseline rate with a constant offer coefficient. The third allows offer interactions and averages paired predictions across all target stores. Keep the sample fixed so that specification changes, rather than changing rows, explain differences.

Exact and coarsened matching make similarity explicit

Matched-target estimates from alternative procedures
MethodMatched adoptersAll adoptersEstimated reduction
Exact on lead and location20262.56
Coarsened baseline + lead + location13262.80
Propensity, logit caliper19263.54

Exact matching here requires the same delivery time and location. Coarsened exact matching additionally puts baseline rates in five-point bands. Within a matched stratum, the comparison mean supplies an outcome for each adopter. Unmatched adopters are excluded, so the reported estimate concerns the retained adopter subset.

A propensity score models adoption, not the outcome

Propensity score e(X) = P(adoption = 1 | pre-policy characteristics X)

The lab fits a regularized logistic model using delivery time, location, and baseline rate. It then finds a nearby nonadopter for each adopter on the logit of that score. A caliper of 0.2 times the score-logit standard deviation limits how far a match may be. Comparisons may be reused.

Inspect overlap before celebrating a match

Fitted adoption-score support
GroupLowest fitted propensityHighest fitted propensity
Adopters0.280.86
Nonadopters0.270.72

The caliper procedure uses 10 distinct comparison stores. Similar scores can still conceal differences in individual covariates. Check the actual matches and report the number excluded; broad score ranges alone do not establish local overlap.

Check balance on the starting variables themselves

Adopter minus comparison; original pooled SD as denominator
VariableStandardized difference beforeAfter propensity matching
lead_days0.880.00
urban-0.09-0.52
baseline_rate0.64-0.24

A standardized mean difference divides the group mean difference by a common scale. The matched calculation weights comparison stores according to how often they are used. Inspect whether the relevant variables became more comparable; do not declare success from the propensity-model fit alone.

Name what the estimate covers

  • Stricter matching excludes adopters. Whose effect is estimated?
Discuss, then reveal

No. Report the matched adopter population and its retained count. Compare its characteristics with the excluded stores. Extending the estimate to all adopters requires an additional argument, not just a different label.

A stricter matching rule excludes several adopters. Can its effect still be presented as the effect for every adopter?

Use matching as a second view of the same comparison

A second procedure pairs each adopter with the closest nonadopter in standardized delivery time, urban location, and baseline rate. The same comparison store can be used more than once. This produces a result for adopters, which should be compared with the model’s adopter average.

The matching estimate for adopters is 2.90 points. Differences from the model estimate lead the analyst back to the actual matches and model specification. The director receives the target population, the paired calculation, and the operational reasons for offering alerts—not a number with an unexplained label.

The next decision concerns a different cohort, whose rollout starts in week 25. Its longer before-and-after record gives us another way to construct a comparison. We will retain the same stockout measure and cost rule.

Update the decision memo

For the 50 voluntary-cohort stores, the adjusted all-store reduction is 3.01 percentage points. The adopter-target estimate is 3.38. Match the reported target to the proposed spending population and carry this evidence alongside the randomized pilot.

Make the call

Why should the matching estimate be compared with the model’s adopter average rather than automatically with its all-store average?

Compare your reasoning

Each match starts from an adopter. It therefore estimates a gain for the adopter mix. The all-store model average gives weight to a different population, including nonadopters.

The bigger picture

A comparison becomes useful when its rows represent the people or sites covered by the decision. Predicting both options for each target store makes that connection visible. The manager can see how changing the rollout population changes the average gain, even when the fitted model stays the same.

After your decision: open the known answer

The known expected reduction for all 50 stores is 3.34 points; for their adopters it is 3.65. Comparing estimates with the matching target separates estimation error from a change in population.
